full_judgment:
2. Mr. M Hafizullah raised question of maintainability of the application for arrest of the vessel 'MT Dolores' on the ground that the Admiralty Court of this Division entertained the plaint illegally as the statements made therein does not disclose any cause of action to attract the jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 and consequently the ad-interim order of arrest was without jurisdiction and the ship is to be released from arrest and the plaint must be rejected. He relied upon section 6. Section 6 is as follows: 

 He put a great stress on the expression "bill of lading" as employed in section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 to contend that "bill of lading" means original bill of lading, a document of title to the property of the cargo and he who holds such original bills of lading the property of the cargo or the goods shipped on board of the vessel passed to him and unless and until the original bills of lading at load ports arc surrendered neither the owner of the vessel nor its master or the local agent is legally bound to issue the delivery order. He submits that in order to invoke section 6 of the Act the statement made in the plaint must disclose damage done to the goods or any part thereof or it must disclose any breach of contract on the part of the owner, master or crew of the ship. From the averments made in this plaint, he submits that plaintiff's case rests on the refusal to pass delivery order for the cargo by the defendant 5 and as the plaintiff failed the defendants 1 and 7 legally refused to issue the delivery order. Mr. Hafizullah, secondly, contends that the statements made in the plaint do not disclose that there is any breach of contract within the meaning of section 6 of the Act. He submits that as there is no cause of action for the suit either on the ground of damage done to the goods or any part thereof by the negligence or misconduct or for any breach of duty or breach of contract the Admiralty Court is not invested with jurisdiction under section 6 of the Act, and the order of arrest was passed upon an illegal assumption of jurisdiction. Thirdly, he contends that in this case as there are conflicting claims over the cargo the ship owner or the Master of the ship cannot issue delivery order for the cargo. 

 3. Dr. Kamal Hossain, on the other hand, relying upon the averments made in the plaint and the documents filed as per list contends that these conclusively prove that the plaintiffs cargo were shipped on board the vessel 'MT Dolores' and the plaintiff has sufficient cause of action for the suit and the Admiralty Court of the High Court Division is invested with jurisdiction under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 to entertain the plaint and to pass the order of arrest and the application for arrest is maintainable. 

 and the case of Stettin (1886-1900) in ASP RMC Vol. 6, 395. Roscoe in his treatise "Admiralty Practise" in Chapter V (4th Edition) said that the claim for damage to the goods by the negligence or misconduct or for any breach of duty or breach of contract on the part of the owner, Master or crew of the ship must be made by the owner or consignee or assignee of the bill of lading of goods. The learned author has also stated that as the right to sue is confined to the owner or consignee or assignee of bill of lading of goods the breach of duty or contract must be in relation to the goods and connected with damage to them. In Stettin it was held that where by a bill of lading goods are to be delivered to a named consignee or his assignee and it is not assigned the master is not justified in delivering to the consignee without his producing the bill of lading and if he does so and the consignee has no right to the possession of the goods, the ship owner is liable to the shipper for damages for wrongful delivery. The decision in the case of Sze Hai Tong Bank Ltd Vs. Rambler Cycle Co. Limited (1959) AC 576 is also to that effect wherein it has been held that the ship owner who delivered without production of the bill of lading does so at his peril. In delivering the goods without production of the bills of lading to a person who to its knowledge was other than one entitled under the bill of lading to receive them the carrier was liable for breach of contract and for conversion. In the above quoted passage from Carver and the principle laid down in these cases I am of the opinion that where the plaintiff in an Admiralty suit fails to produce the original bill of lading the owners of the ship or the master of the vessel or the agent of the ship cannot give delivery order of the cargo and if it is so given then the carrier shall be liable for breach of contract. In view of the language employed in section 6 of the Act I am of the opinion that in order to invoke the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 two conditions are to be satisfied from the averments of the plaint, one is the damage done to the goods on board ship by negligence or misconduct of the owner, master or crews of the ship and the other, breach of contract in relation to the cargo shipped into vessel for carriage to the port of discharge. This view of mine finds support from the observation made in Al-Sayar Navigation Co. Vs. Delta International Trader Limited and others, 34 DLR 110 (AD). The relevant passage is found in paragraph 8 of the judgment. In the instant case the plaintiff is not entitled in law to have an order of delivery of the cargo from the master of the ship or for that matter from defendant 1 or from the agent defendant 5 of the owner of the ship as it failed to produce the original bills of lading. In this case before us it appears that the local agent of the owner of the ship even made a declaration under section 55 (E) of the Customs Act, 1969 and by making such declaration the agent of the defendant 1 is under legal duty to deliver the goods to the plaintiffs on production of valid documents. The defendant 5 has issued the letter not to deliver the cargo for not surrendering of the original bills of lading and that was not opposed to law. 

 14. Dr. Kamal Hossain lastly, argues that section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 is a remedial measure and requires liberal construction. So contending he urges that the suit and order of arrest is maintainable. The contention on remedial measure and liberal construction of section 6 of the Act admits of no doubt. But that does not help Dr. Kamal Hossain as the cause of action for the suit is absent as already has been stated above. Therefore, in view of the aforesaid discussion, I am of the opinion that I assumed jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court not vested in me under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 on the facts as disclosed in the plaint and the documents filed by the parties. 

 15. Although the application is filed for rejection of the plaint but I return the plaint to the filing advocate in exercise of the inherent power as contemplated under section 151 CPC as there is no cause of action to try the suit as this Admiralty Court is lacking jurisdiction without rejecting the same as the Admiralty Court cannot reject the plaint as the provision of Civil Procedure Code of rejecting the plaint have not been made applicable to Admiralty Court nor under the Rule of Admiralty Court such order can be made. This view of mine finds support from the decision in the case of Sakh Steel Industries Ltd. Vs. TSS Pacific Abdo and others 35 DLR 188 (AD).
